analysis.one_liner: Raises fuel economy standards for light trucks, heavier vehicles, and the federal fleet.
analysis.headline: The Automobile Fuel Economy Act of 2001 never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from May 2001 until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required automakers to steadily raise the average fuel economy of their light trucks — SUVs and pickups — from about 20 mpg to 27.5 mpg by model year 2007, closed a loophole that let the heaviest vehicles off the hook, and required federal agencies to buy more efficient vehicles. Drivers would save money at the gas pump; automakers would have had to build more efficient trucks. The Senate never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who buys or drives a car, SUV, or pickup: higher fuel economy standards mean vehicles that go farther on a gallon of gas, lowering fuel bills year after year. Drivers of light trucks stood to gain the most, since that category had lagged far behind cars. Reduced gasoline consumption also modestly lowered the country's oil dependence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, especially SUV and pickup owners

how_it_helps.text: It phases the light-truck fuel economy standard up to 27.5 miles per gallon by model year 2007, with intermediate steps of 22.5 mpg by 2005 and 25 mpg by 2007 — the same standard cars already meet.
It redefines an 'automobile' to cover vehicles up to 10,000 pounds gross vehicle weight starting in 2007, bringing the largest SUVs within fuel economy rules they currently escape.
It requires every federal agency's new vehicle purchases to average at least 3 mpg better than its fiscal 2001 baseline by 2003 and 6 mpg better by 2005, saving taxpayer money on fuel.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, particularly those selling large numbers of SUVs and pickups, would bear the engineering cost of meeting the higher standards. Those costs would be passed at least partly to buyers through vehicle prices, though that would be partly offset by lower fuel spending over each vehicle's life.

drawbacks.text: Meeting a 27.5 mpg light-truck standard requires real engineering investment — redesigned drivetrains, lighter materials, more efficient engines — and automakers argued those costs would raise sticker prices for the truck and SUV buyers the rules target.

The transition schedules were fixed in statute, which gives manufacturers less flexibility than a regulatory process that can adjust targets to costs; buyers who specifically wanted large, powerful vehicles would see fewer choices or higher prices during the phase-in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most drivers, lower fuel spending over the life of a vehicle outweighs a modest price increase, and the bill attacked the biggest gap in fuel economy law: light trucks — SUVs and pickups — were held to a far weaker standard than cars. The heaviest 10,000-pound vehicles would not have been covered until 2007, and the federal fleet provisions are small relative to the overall market. On balance the public benefit was large and the cost was concentrated on manufacturers and buyers of the largest vehicles.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on May 1, 2001, with Senator Olympia Snowe, a Republican, among its original cosponsors, giving it support from both parties from the start.
Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill — 10 Democrats and 4 Republicans.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced; the committee took no further action on it.
No vote was ever held in the Senate, and the bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers, above all those whose profits depended on large SUVs and pickups, were better off because the bill never became law — they avoided a mandate to bring light trucks up to the car standard of 27.5 mpg. Gasoline sellers also avoided a long-term decline in fuel demand.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Automobile Fuel Economy Act of 2001 and gave introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan support at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over fuel economy standards
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out, held no markup, and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: U.S. automakers
against.role: Manufacturers of light trucks and SUVs
against.what_they_did: Opposed raising light-truck fuel economy standards during the 2001-2002 debate, and Congress instead approved a modest study of fuel economy rather than an increase.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so there is no roll call to judge by; its 14 cosponsors split 10 Democrats and 4 Republicans, and a Republican — Senator Olympia Snowe of Maine — was among the original cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers to raise the average fuel economy of light trucks to 27.5 mpg — the standard cars already met — and to bring vehicles up to 10,000 pounds into the rules. Automakers' interest in avoiding the engineering cost ran against drivers' interest in cheaper fuel bills.
Higher fuel economy means less gasoline sold over time. Any industry interest in preserving fuel demand ran against consumers' interest in spending less at the pump.
Agencies would have had to buy fleets averaging 3 mpg better by 2003 and 6 mpg better by 2005 — a front-loaded purchasing cost offset by lower fuel spending and a smaller taxpayer footprint.
